items.title: Funding for-profits with charitable dollars
items.content:
One common objection to impact-focused for-profits is that for-profits won’t be able to access the incoming torrent of philanthropic funding. But this doesn’t have to be true! There are lots of ways that charitable dollars can be directed to for-profits, and Manifund and other funders do it regularly.

There are four general categories of options—here’s why you might want to do each:

### TL;DR

- Is there no realistic path to revenue/growth, or is the amount small? → grant
- Is there high growth potential? → investment
- Is there predictable revenue or future grants, but not high growth potential? → loan (or revenue-share investment)
- Do you want to pay for a specific output rather than supporting the organization as a whole? → commission

### Grants

You can give charitable funding as a grant to a for-profit, as long as it’s for a scoped charitable purpose and the grant has appropriate restrictions and oversight. Practically speaking, Manifund likes doing this if it’s a smaller amount (eg <$50k) such that it’s not worth doing more complicated paperwork, or if it’s a project where we don’t expect a ton of revenue, growth, or follow-on equity funding.

This is often the case for media, a classic public good. Some examples include Coefficient Giving giving around $2.6m to Should We Studio, a for-profit video production company making animated content about EA concepts. Vox’s Future Perfect has also gotten funding from philanthropic sources like the Rockefeller Foundation (a founding grant of $380k), Animal Charity Evaluators, and the BEMC Foundation.

Outside media, CG, EA Funds, and Jaan Tallinn have all given grants to Metaculus. Metaculus is a for-profit (specifically a public benefit corporation), but not one particularly oriented toward revenue or growth, and most of its funding has come from grants....

items.title: AAR 9/29: Public Sector AI Symposium Ottawa (AWS+Accenture+Anthropic), Policy Foresight Afternoon (Center for International Governance Innovation), Versaterm Users Conference (Police, Fire, Emergency), GCXpo at Area X.O (Department of National Defence), and VCF Cluster Access (Lucid Computing)
items.content:
# Executive Summary

- This report covers a recent visit to the Capital City of Canada. Location(s): The Westin Hotel, CF Rideau Centre, Colonel By Hall uOttawa. Duration of trip: 13 hours and 15 minutes. Time period: From 7:25 to 20:40 on September 29, 2026.
- Primary objective(s): reconnaissance and intelligence gathering. Morning: Skip GCXpo to sleep: OODA loop said risk-reward tradeoff of going 15 km south then back was not worth it. I got called several times during my naps so this wasn't nearly as restful as I'd hoped. Scout Art Gallery of Ottawa: Packing, investigate attendee list, rehearse and study list of 14 shovel ready technical project ideas in compute verification, courtesy of Luke Marks (Martian). I considered a direct approach to Parliament Hall in case I could have a hallway chat with someone about verification but decided it'd risk greatly reducing my credibility if it wasn't well planned out (e.g a preexisting appointment at the bare minimum), easier to call a representative, but very much not my comparative advantage. Afternoon: Lucid Computing meeting: attend office hour, intro, sign deal, get GPUs. CIGI Panel discussions: had to leave in the middle to get a power bank. My mistake was that I wasted time trying to find one on campus after salah at multi-faith centre, I should have gone to Rideau Centre directly. I judged that asking for consent to record may risk violating a social norm, but I lost the notes I took before saving them into persistent storage. People in the room said I came across as intense. Department of National Defence: walk-in, request process to apply for building pass, they get very confused after I clarify that I'm not a defense contractor or government employee in any capacity, just a researcher that wants to work with legitimate authorities to protect Canadians from AI risks, and has relevant expertise and experience for doing so successfully. I show them the business card of my contact, he doesn't pick up the phone, so...

items.title: How to Cope with the Destruction of Everything you Know and Love
items.content:
What seems like forever ago, I had lunch with Yudkowsky during Manifest 2023. He told me that he thought there was a 99% chance that AI would cause human extinction. That was the beginning of a year-long hiatus from the rationalist community. It simply brought too much anxiety. The cruel march of time continues nonetheless, and I have been forced to accept that existential risk is a topic that I must engage with, at my peril.

It is bittersweet to be human. Our cognition allows us to experience beauty, find love, make friends; yet, it also brings us awareness of our own mortality. Over the past months, I've been exploring what happens to a person's psychology when they are faced with "the end", especially on a civilizational level. This is indeed a deeply personal journey for me, but the topic is universal, so I hope that my findings are meaningful to you. AI risk is what specifically motivated this journey, but the lessons are nonetheless applicable to any form of civilizational-scale risk.

There is indeed no "correct" emotional response to existential risk. Neither is there a correct motivation: some people are more concerned with their own end than that of civilization, and vice versa.

Yudkowsky has indeed written about his take on how he copes with the end of the world. I think his take is perfectly valid. My name is also not Yudkowsky, and I think that he and I have very different minds. What brought me back to engaging with existential risk was not reading rationalist theory, but rather consuming media, finding love, and making friends. I have more doom and more hope than I have ever had before....

items.title: Limited virtual currency as a way of understanding specialization in humans
items.content:
Why do we need to specialize? Our time is limited, we cannot do everything and need focussed efforts into a few things. How do we decide what we want to focus on?

I was recently going through virtual economies paper and the auctions setting particularly interested me. Agents are given equal virtual currency and they need to bid on tasks based on whatever they want the most. Suppose I as an agent A want X, Y, Z the most compared to others (X2, Y2, Z2..) and I will divide my bids based on proportion of my desirability of X, Y, Z placing the bids on highest desired outcomes.

Another agent wants something else and will place bid according to his preferences. Since the currency is limited, an agent cannot get/do everything and has to choose. Whatever he chooses and does kind of changes his skills and outlook in life and its a cyclic process - decide bids based on desirability -> get your allocations -> changes in desirability based on outcomes/goal satisfaction/alignment with values -> place next bids...

Is this true for us? We have limited (probably not equal) currency in terms of our time and energy. If I want to focus on sports, I will give more preference to sports and dedicate more time to it. We divide our currency (time) according to our preferences among several outcomes. We probably cannot do everything all at once and need to bid (allocate time) based on the things we want the most (maybe due to more rewards in terms of finances, learning, our inherent values, passion, etc).

This probably explains why humans specialise in (few) occupations (doctors, teachers, engineers, scientists, sports-persons, actors etc) and put focussed efforts on one or few fields. One can be a master of few or many since some learnings can transfer but cannot possibly be a master of all trades.

items.summary: A speculative post drawing an analogy between auction-based virtual economies for AI agents (equal currency, preference-driven bidding on tasks) and human specialization, proposing that limited time and energy function like limited currency in a cyclic bidding-allocation-desirability process. It connects alignment-relevant virtual economy research to a folk model of human goal formation.

items.title: Self as sub-selves vs groups of individuals
items.content:
Our mind contains representations (perfect/imperfect) of the world. When someone is able to understand and control their mind, it is said they can understand and conquer the world (in spirituality).

Why so?

Probably pico-economics has an answer. It describes self has conflicting sub-selves with conflicting goals.

Did you ever wonder on what to do next and were stuck between different conflicting choices? What was going on in your head at that time?

There was a battle between parts of you who wanted different things. The fitness freak self probably wanted to go to gym in evening, social self wanted to hang-out with friends, workaholic self wanted to just work on the project, nerd self wanted to read a book/article or explorer self who wanted to visit a new place? What did you act on? Probably the self that won in the conflict: maybe the one that was most aligned with your current goals (maybe you decided to loose weight and prioritised fitness-freak self's suggestion). But who decided your goals? was it you or a coalition of your selves who gave different suggestions on which goals to prioritise? did your goals change over time? You wanted to become an astronaut in childhood and now want to do X, 2 years later you decided to do Y, become Z.

So, can it be said that we consist of evolving selves who are in constant battle with each other and the one that wins governs our next actions. Once we take those actions, based on the reward we get, our sub-selves who prove that their suggested goals and actions are more aligned maybe in terms of better reward (internal or external)) are acted upon and drive our goal setting. Maybe our goals are a mix of different goals of these sub-selves....

It is reflective philosophical writing rather than analysis of AI systems.
